claim: In natural populations of Podospora anserina, seven spore killer types (Psks) have been identified through classical genetic analyses.
source: In natural populations of Podospora anserina, seven spore killer types (Psks) have been identified through classical genetic analyses.
evidence: This is stated directly in the abstract and is supported by citation to previous work (van der Gaag et al., 2000).

claim: The Spok gene family underlies the Psks.
source: Here we show that the Spok gene family underlies the Psks.
evidence: This is a primary finding of the study, supported by experimental data presented throughout the manuscript.

claim: The combination of Spok genes at different chromosomal locations defines the spore killer types and creates a killing hierarchy within a population.
source: The combination of Spok genes at different chromosomal locations defines the spore killer types and creates a killing hierarchy within a population.
evidence: This is a primary finding supported by genomic and crossing data presented in the manuscript.

claim: Two novel Spok homologs (Spok3 and Spok4) were identified.
source: We identify two novel Spok homologs located within a large (74–167 kbp) region (the Spok block) that resides in different chromosomal locations in different strains.
evidence: This is a primary finding of the study, supported by genomic sequencing and analysis.

claim: Spok3 and Spok4 are located within a large (74–167 kbp) region called the Spok block.
source: We identify two novel Spok homologs located within a large (74–167 kbp) region (the Spok block) that resides in different chromosomal locations in different strains.
evidence: This is supported by genomic assembly and alignment data.

claim: The Spok block resides in different chromosomal locations in different strains.
source: We identify two novel Spok homologs located within a large (74–167 kbp) region (the Spok block) that resides in different chromosomal locations in different strains.
evidence: This is supported by genomic data and Table 1 showing different chromosomal locations.

claim: The SPOK protein performs both killing and resistance functions.
source: We confirm that the SPOK protein performs both killing and resistance functions and show that these activities are dependent on distinct domains, a predicted nuclease and kinase domain.
evidence: This is confirmed through experimental data including knock-in/knock-out experiments and domain analysis.

claim: The killing and resistance activities of SPOK are dependent on distinct domains: a predicted nuclease and kinase domain.
source: We confirm that the SPOK protein performs both killing and resistance functions and show that these activities are dependent on distinct domains, a predicted nuclease and kinase domain.
evidence: This is supported by experimental data from domain mutagenesis and functional assays.

claim: Genomic and phylogenetic analyses across ascomycetes suggest that the Spok genes disperse through cross-species transfer.
source: Genomic and phylogenetic analyses across ascomycetes suggest that the Spok genes disperse through cross-species transfer, and evolve by duplication and diversification within lineages.
evidence: This is supported by phylogenetic analysis showing incongruence between species and gene trees.

claim: Spok genes evolve by duplication and diversification within lineages.
source: Genomic and phylogenetic analyses across ascomycetes suggest that the Spok genes disperse through cross-species transfer, and evolve by duplication and diversification within lineages.
evidence: This is supported by the presence of multiple copies in genomes and phylogenetic patterns.

claim: Meiotic drivers use a variety of mechanisms to hijack meiosis in order to bias their transmission to the gametes in proportions greater than 50%.
source: These elements use a variety of mechanisms to hijack meiosis in order to bias their transmission to the gametes in proportions greater than 50% (Sandler and Novitski, 1957).
evidence: This is established knowledge in the field, supported by citation.

claim: Spore killing represents the most direct way to observe the presence of drive.
source: In ascomycete fungi, meiotic drive occurs in the form of spore killing, which represents the most direct way to observe the presence of drive (Turner and Perkins, 1991).
evidence: This is stated as established knowledge with citation support.

claim: When a strain possessing a driving allele mates with a compatible strain that does not carry the allele, the meiotic products that carry the driving allele will induce the abortion of their sibling spores that do not have the allele.
source: When a strain possessing a driving allele mates with a compatible strain that does not carry the allele (i.e., a sensitive strain), the meiotic products (ascospores) that carry the driving allele will induce the abortion of their sibling spores that do not have the allele.
evidence: This describes the mechanism of spore killing, supported by established knowledge and citations.

claim: Spore killing results in half of the normal number of viable spores.
source: Spore killing is apparent in the sexual structures (asci) of the fungi because it results in half of the normal number of viable spores.
evidence: This is an observable phenotype described in the manuscript and supported by established knowledge.

claim: Spore killing is unusual among meiotic drivers as it is the only system in which the offspring of an organism are killed by the drive.
source: Owing to the haplontic life cycle of most fungi, spore killing is unusual among meiotic drivers as it is the only system in which the offspring of an organism are killed by the drive (Lyttle, 1991).
evidence: This is stated as a distinguishing feature with citation support.

claim: With few exceptions, spore killer elements appear to be governed by single loci that confer both killing and resistance.
source: In addition, with few exceptions (Hammond et al., 2012; Svedberg et al., 2018), spore killer elements appear to be governed by single loci that confer both killing and resistance (Grognet et al., 2014; Nuckolls et al., 2017; Hu et al., 2017), which contrasts with the other well-studied drive systems that comprise genomic regions as large as entire chromosomes (Larracuente and Presgraves, 2012; Hammer et al., 1989).
evidence: This is stated as established knowledge with multiple citations.

claim: Natural populations of Podospora anserina are known to host multiple spore killers.
source: Natural populations of the filamentous fungus Podospora anserina are known to host multiple spore killers (Grognet et al., 2014; van der Gaag et al., 2000; Hamann and Osiewacz, 2004), and hence provide an ideal system for the investigation of interactions among drivers at the population level.
evidence: This is stated with citation support from previous studies.

claim: The first spore killer gene to be described in P. anserina was het-s.
source: The first spore killer gene to be described in P. anserina was het-s, a gene that is also involved in allorecognition (Dalstra et al., 2003).
evidence: This is stated as historical fact with citation.

claim: het-s is also involved in allorecognition.
source: The first spore killer gene to be described in P. anserina was het-s, a gene that is also involved in allorecognition (Dalstra et al., 2003).
evidence: This is stated with citation support.

claim: Spok1 is only known from a single representative of P. comata.
source: Spok1 is only known from a single representative of P. comata, a species that is closely related to P. anserina, whereas Spok2 has been shown to exist in high frequency among strains of a French population of P. anserina (Grognet et al., 2014).
evidence: This is stated with citation support.

claim: Spok2 exists in high frequency among strains of a French population of P. anserina.
source: Spok1 is only known from a single representative of P. comata, a species that is closely related to P. anserina, whereas Spok2 has been shown to exist in high frequency among strains of a French population of P. anserina (Grognet et al., 2014).
evidence: This is stated with citation support.

claim: Spok1 is capable of killing in the presence of Spok2, but not vice versa.
source: Spok1 is capable of killing in the presence of Spok2, but not vice versa, indicating a dominant epistatic relationship between the two genes.
evidence: This is stated with implicit citation to Grognet et al., 2014.

claim: There is a dominant epistatic relationship between Spok1 and Spok2.
source: Spok1 is capable of killing in the presence of Spok2, but not vice versa, indicating a dominant epistatic relationship between the two genes.
evidence: This is inferred from the killing pattern described.

claim: Seven spore killer genotypes (Psk-1 through Psk-7) have been identified through classical genetic analysis.
source: In addition, seven spore killer genotypes have been identified through classical genetic analysis (van der Gaag et al., 2000). These are referred to as Psk-1 through Psk-7 and were defined by observing the presence, absence and frequency of killed spores in defined crosses among French and Dutch P. anserina strains (Box 1—figure 1).
evidence: This is stated with citation support.

claim: The het-s gene itself is not associated with the Psks.
source: The het-s gene itself is not associated with the Psks, but allorecognition is correlated with Psk spore killing (van der Gaag et al., 2003).
evidence: This is stated with citation support.

claim: Allorecognition is correlated with Psk spore killing.
source: The het-s gene itself is not associated with the Psks, but allorecognition is correlated with Psk spore killing (van der Gaag et al., 2003).
evidence: This is stated with citation support.

claim: High-quality whole-genome assemblies were generated using a combination of long-read (PacBio and MinION Oxford Nanopore) and short-read (Illumina HiSeq) technologies.
source: To investigate the genetic basis of spore killing in P. anserina, we generated high-quality whole-genome assemblies using a combination of long-read (PacBio and MinION Oxford Nanopore) and short-read (Illumina HiSeq) technologies.
evidence: This describes the methods used in the study.

claim: The final assemblies recovered the expected seven chromosomes in their entirety for five strains.
source: The final assemblies (long-read technologies polished with Illumina HiSeq data) recovered the expected seven chromosomes in their entirety for five strains, and in up to 13 scaffolds for the rest (Supplementary file 1).
evidence: This is a result of the genomic assembly work.

claim: BUSCO analyses of the assemblies reported 97–98% of 3725 Sordariomyceta-conserved genes.
source: BUSCO analyses of these assemblies reported 97–98% of 3725 Sordariomyceta-conserved genes (Supplementary file 1), which is concordant with the same analysis done in the reference assemblies of the P. anserina strain S+ (hereafter referred to as Podan2; Espagne et al., 2008) and of P. comata (PODCO; Silar et al., 2019).
evidence: This is a quality metric for the genome assemblies.

claim: The P. anserina samples are remarkably similar to each other and distinct from those of both P. comata and P. pauciseta.
source: A NeighborNet split network of 1000 single-copy orthologs (including introns) showed that the P. anserina samples are remarkably similar to each other and distinct from those of both P. comata and P. pauciseta (Figure 1A).
evidence: This is supported by phylogenetic analysis shown in Figure 1A.

claim: The average genic identity within P. anserina is 99.97%.
source: Nevertheless, the three taxa are very closely related: the average genic identity within P. anserina is 99.97%, whereas the genic distance between P. anserina and P. pauciseta is 99.10%, between P. anserina and P. comata is 98.87%, and between P. pauciseta and P. comata is 98.79%.
evidence: This is a quantitative result from sequence analysis.

claim: The genic distance between P. anserina and P. pauciseta is 99.10%.
source: Nevertheless, the three taxa are very closely related: the average genic identity within P. anserina is 99.97%, whereas the genic distance between P. anserina and P. pauciseta is 99.10%, between P. anserina and P. comata is 98.87%, and between P. pauciseta and P. comata is 98.79%.
evidence: This is a quantitative result from sequence analysis.

claim: The genic distance between P. anserina and P. comata is 98.87%.
source: Nevertheless, the three taxa are very closely related: the average genic identity within P. anserina is 99.97%, whereas the genic distance between P. anserina and P. pauciseta is 99.10%, between P. anserina and P. comata is 98.87%, and between P. pauciseta and P. comata is 98.79%.
evidence: This is a quantitative result from sequence analysis.

claim: The genic distance between P. pauciseta and P. comata is 98.79%.
source: Nevertheless, the three taxa are very closely related: the average genic identity within P. anserina is 99.97%, whereas the genic distance between P. anserina and P. pauciseta is 99.10%, between P. anserina and P. comata is 98.87%, and between P. pauciseta and P. comata is 98.79%.
evidence: This is a quantitative result from sequence analysis.

claim: Whole-genome alignments recovered strongly conserved synteny at the chromosomal level when small (<13 kb) translocations are excluded.
source: Accordingly, the whole-genome alignments recovered strongly conserved synteny at the chromosomal level when small (<13 kb) translocations (presumably due to transposable elements (TEs)) are excluded (Figure 1B; Figure 1—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is supported by alignment data shown in Figure 1B.

claim: Only three larger translocations were detected between the Podospora species.
source: Only three larger translocations were detected, of which two might be mis-assemblies in the reference genome of P. comata (PODCO; see 'Materials and methods').
evidence: This is a result from genome alignment analysis.

claim: Spok2 is present on the left arm of chromosome 5 in the majority of strains.
source: By searching our assemblies for the Spok2 sequence (presented by Grognet et al., 2014) using BLAST, we confirm the presence of this Spok gene on the left arm of chromosome 5 in the majority of strains, in agreement with Grognet et al. (2014).
evidence: This is confirmed by BLAST searches and agrees with previous work.

claim: Two novel homologs (Spok3 and Spok4) were identified based on sequence similarity with Spok2.
source: Furthermore, on the basis of sequence similarity with Spok2, we identified two novel homologs that we refer to as Spok3 and Spok4.
evidence: This is a primary finding from sequence analysis.

claim: Spok3 and Spok4 are found at different genomic locations depending on the strain.
source: These newly identified Spoks are found at different genomic locations depending on the strain. Both Spok3 and Spok4 can be located on the left arm of chromosome 3 or on the left arm of chromosome 5, and Spok3 can be found at an additional location on the right arm of chromosome 5.
evidence: This is supported by genomic data in Table 1.

claim: A pseudogenized Spok gene (SpokΨ1) was found in the subtelomeric region of the right arm of chromosome 5.
source: In addition, the BLAST searches recovered a pseudogenized Spok gene (SpokΨ1) in the subtelomeric region of the right arm of chromosome 5.
evidence: This is a finding from BLAST searches.

claim: The Spok homologs show a high degree of conservation, including the 3' and 5' UTRs.
source: Overall they show a high degree of conservation, including the 3' and 5' UTRs.
evidence: This is based on sequence alignment analysis.

claim: A nucleotide alignment of the Spok genes' coding sequence revealed 130 variable sites out of 2334 total sites.
source: A nucleotide alignment of the Spok genes' coding sequence revealed 130 variable sites out of 2334 total sites (Figure 2—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is a quantitative result from sequence alignment.

claim: 67% of the variable sites result in amino acid changes.
source: A relatively large proportion (67%, 87/130) of those variable sites result in amino acid changes and 74% are unique to one of the Spok homologs.
evidence: This is a quantitative result from sequence analysis.

claim: 74% of variable sites are unique to one of the Spok homologs.
source: A relatively large proportion (67%, 87/130) of those variable sites result in amino acid changes and 74% are unique to one of the Spok homologs.
evidence: This is a quantitative result from sequence analysis.

claim: There are six indels among all the Spok genes.
source: There are six indels among all the Spok genes, including one at the 5' end of the ORF that represents a variable-length repeat region, and one at the 3' end of the ORF that is shared by Spok3 and Spok4.
evidence: This is based on sequence alignment analysis.

claim: The 3' end indel induces a frameshift and changes the position of the stop codon.
source: The 3' end indel induces a frameshift and changes the position of the stop codon (Figure 2A).
evidence: This is shown in Figure 2A.

claim: SpokΨ1 has a missing 5' end, multiple stop codons, and a discoglosse DNA transposon inserted in the coding region.
source: SpokΨ1 has a missing 5' end, multiple stop codons, and a discoglosse (Tc1/mariner-like) DNA transposon (Espagne et al., 2008) inserted in the coding region.
evidence: This is based on sequence analysis.

claim: SpokΨ1 has no deletions relative to the other Spok homologs.
source: Of particular interest, SpokΨ1 has no deletions relative to the other Spok homologs, suggesting that the indels in the functional Spok homologs represent derived deletions.
evidence: This is based on sequence alignment and leads to an inference about evolution.

claim: The indels in the functional Spok homologs represent derived deletions.
source: Of particular interest, SpokΨ1 has no deletions relative to the other Spok homologs, suggesting that the indels in the functional Spok homologs represent derived deletions.
evidence: This is inferred from the comparison with SpokΨ1.

claim: There is little allelic variation within the Spok homologs in the Wageningen population.
source: There is little allelic variation within the Spok homologs in the Wageningen population and the variants of the four homologs cluster phylogenetically (Figure 2B and C).
evidence: This is supported by phylogenetic analysis shown in Figure 2B and C.

claim: The variants of the four Spok homologs cluster phylogenetically.
source: There is little allelic variation within the Spok homologs in the Wageningen population and the variants of the four homologs cluster phylogenetically (Figure 2B and C).
evidence: This is shown in Figure 2B and C.

claim: The Spok2 gene in the Wageningen strains are identical to the two alleles described in Grognet et al. (2014), with the exception of Spok2 from Wa58– which has a single SNP that results in a D358N substitution.
source: The Spok2 gene in the Wageningen strains are identical to the two alleles described in Grognet et al. (2014), with the exception of Spok2 from Wa58– which has a single SNP that results in a D358N substitution.
evidence: This is based on sequence comparison.

claim: Spok3 has five allelic variants.
source: Spok3 has five allelic variants, and the allelic variation of Spok4 is reminiscent of Spok2, with only Wa100+ and Wa58– having a single synonymous SNP (Figure 2C).
evidence: This is based on sequence analysis shown in Figure 2C.

claim: The three copies of SpokΨ1 are all unique.
source: Lastly, the three copies of SpokΨ1 are all unique.
evidence: This is based on sequence comparison.

claim: A number of the allelic variants of Spok3 show signatures of gene conversion events.
source: Notably, a number of the allelic variants of Spok3 show signatures of gene conversion events (Lazzaro and Clark, 2001).
evidence: This is inferred from sequence patterns and supported by citation to methods.

claim: Strain Y+ has three SNPs near the start of the Spok3 gene that result in amino-acid changes and that match those in Spok2 exactly.
source: Specifically, strain Y+ has three SNPs near the start of the gene that result in amino-acid changes and that match those in Spok2 exactly (Figure 2—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 1.

claim: The Wa53+ allele of Spok3 has a series of SNPs (a track of 205 bp) that are identical to those in Spok4 but different from all other Spok3 sequences.
source: The Wa53+ allele of Spok3 has a series of SNPs (a track of 205 bp) that are identical to those in Spok4 but different from all other Spok3 sequences, and three additional SNPs near the 5' end that also match Spok4 (Figure 2—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 1.

claim: The TG+ strain possesses two identical copies of Spok3.
source: The TG+ strain possesses two identical copies of Spok3 (see 'Materials and methods') that share the aforementioned tract with Wa53+, but which extends for an additional 217 bp (Figure 2—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is based on sequence analysis shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 1.

claim: The gene conversion events between Spok homologs are supported by the reticulation shown in a NeighborNet split network.
source: The gene conversion events between Spok homologs are supported by the reticulation shown in a NeighborNet split network (Figure 2B) and by a significant recombination Phi test (199 informative sites, p=1.528e-12).
evidence: This is supported by phylogenetic analysis and statistical test.

claim: A significant recombination Phi test supports gene conversion events between Spok homologs (199 informative sites, p=1.528e-12).
source: The gene conversion events between Spok homologs are supported by the reticulation shown in a NeighborNet split network (Figure 2B) and by a significant recombination Phi test (199 informative sites, p=1.528e-12).
evidence: This is a statistical result from recombination analysis.

claim: A maximum likelihood phylogenetic analysis of the UTR sequences suggests that Spok3 and Spok4 are closely related.
source: A maximum likelihood phylogenetic analysis of the UTR sequences (defined by conservation across homologs) suggests that Spok3 and Spok4 are closely related (Figure 2C), which is at odds with the high structural similarity of the coding sequences of Spok1 and Spok4 (Figure 2A).
evidence: This is shown in Figure 2C.

claim: The absence of Spok2 in some strains is a result of a one-time deletion.
source: In the few strains with no copy of Spok2, analysis of the region suggests that this is a result of a one-time deletion (Figure 3).
evidence: This is inferred from sequence analysis shown in Figure 3.

claim: The absence of Spok2 constitutes a deletion, rather than the ancestral state within P. anserina.
source: This configuration implies that the absence of Spok2 constitutes a deletion (3), rather than the ancestral state within P. anserina.
evidence: This is inferred from the pattern of transposable elements in the region.

claim: Spok1 was previously identified from the P. comata strain TD.
source: The Spok1 gene was previously identified from the P. comata strain TD (Grognet et al., 2014).
evidence: This is stated with citation.

claim: No other strains investigated in this study possess Spok1.
source: No other strains investigated in this study were found to possess Spok1, indicating that this gene is probably not present in P. anserina.
evidence: This is based on BLAST searches of the sequenced genomes.

claim: Spok1 is probably not present in P. anserina.
source: No other strains investigated in this study were found to possess Spok1, indicating that this gene is probably not present in P. anserina.
evidence: This is inferred from the absence in all P. anserina strains sequenced.

claim: The genome of P. pauciseta strain CBS237.71 contains both Spok3 and Spok4.
source: The sequencing reveals that the genome of the P. pauciseta strain CBS237.71 contains both Spok3 and Spok4 (Table 1; Figure 2B), but they are at a genomic location that differs from those in any of the P. anserina strains.
evidence: This is shown in Table 1 and Figure 2B.

claim: Spok3 and Spok4 in P. pauciseta are at a genomic location that differs from those in any of the P. anserina strains.
source: The sequencing reveals that the genome of the P. pauciseta strain CBS237.71 contains both Spok3 and Spok4 (Table 1; Figure 2B), but they are at a genomic location that differs from those in any of the P. anserina strains.
evidence: This is based on genomic location data in Table 1.

claim: Spok3 and Spok4 function as meiotic drive genes.
source: We constructed knock-in and knock-out strains to confirm that the newly discovered Spok homologs, Spok3 and Spok4, can induce spore killing on their own (Supplementary file 3), as previously shown for Spok2 by Grognet et al. (2014).
evidence: This is confirmed by experimental crosses described in the text.

claim: Both Spok3::PaPKS1 ΔSpok2 x ΔSpok2 and Spok4::PaPKS1 ΔSpok2 x ΔSpok2 crosses yielded almost 100% two-spored asci with two white spores.
source: Accordingly, both Spok3::PaPKS1 ΔSpok2 x ΔSpok2 and Spok4::PaPKS1 ΔSpok2 x ΔSpok2 crosses yielded almost 100% two-spored asci with two white spores (118/119, 99.1%; Figure 4—figure supplement 2C) and (343/346, 99.1%; Figure 4—figure supplement 2D), respectively.
evidence: This is experimental data shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 2C and D.

claim: Spok3 and Spok4 function as spore killers when introduced as a single copy at the PaPKS1 locus.
source: These results show that Spok3 and Spok4 function as spore killers when introduced as a single copy at the PaPKS1 locus .
evidence: This is concluded from the experimental crosses.

claim: The cross between Spok3::PaPKS1d and Spok4::PaPKS1 yielded asci that had four aborted spores, indicating mutual killing of Spok3 and Spok4.
source: The cross between Spok3::PaPKS1d and Spok4::PaPKS1 yielded asci that had four aborted spores, indicating mutual killing of Spok3 and Spok4 (Figure 4—figure supplement 2G).
evidence: This is experimental data shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 2G.

claim: Spok3 kills in the presence of Spok2.
source: This cross yielded mostly two-spored asci with two unpigmented spores (163/165 asci: 98.8%) (Figure 4—figure supplement 2H), indicating that Spok3 kills in the presence of Spok2.
evidence: This is experimental data from crosses.

claim: Spok4 kills in the presence of Spok2.
source: Similarly, to determine the killing relation between Spok2 and Spok4, a cross was conducted between Spok4::PaPKS1 and s, which resulted in 99:5% killing (216/217 asci) (Figure 4—figure supplement 2I).
evidence: This is experimental data from crosses.

claim: Spok2 does not confer resistance to Spok3 and Spok4.
source: Although these two crosses indicate that Spok2 does not confer resistance to Spok3 and Spok4 (Spok3 and Spok4 both kill Spok2), they do not allow us to determine whether Spok3 or Spok4 confer resistance to Spok2.
evidence: This is inferred from the crossing results.

claim: Spok2 killing occurs in the presence of Spok3.
source: To address this point, Spok2 killing was analyzed in a cross that was homoallelic for Spok3 (Spok3::PaPKS1 x Spok3::PaPKS1d ΔSpok2), which yielded 46% two-spored asci (143/310), confirming that Spok2 killing occurs in the presence of Spok3 (Figure 4—figure supplement 2J).
evidence: This is experimental data from crosses.

claim: Spok4 does not confer resistance to Spok2 killing.
source: Finally, to determine whether Spok4 is resistant to Spok2, we made a Spok4::PaPKS1 x Spok4::PaPKS1 ΔSpok2 cross, which resulted in 11/24 two-spored asci (Figure 4—figure supplement 2K). Although this genetic background is ill-suited for determining killing frequency (because of the aforementioned effect of the homozygous PaPKS1 deletion on fertility), the presence of two-spore asci suggests that Spok4 does not confer resistance to Spok2 killing.
evidence: This is inferred from experimental data.

claim: Spok2, Spok3, and Spok4 do not interact.
source: Overall, these results indicate that Spok2, Spok3, and Spok4 do not interact.
evidence: This is concluded from the series of crossing experiments.

claim: The backcrossed strain Psk5xS5 has neither a Psk-5 nor a Psk-S phenotype, but a Psk-1 phenotype.
source: Notably, crossing results reveal that Psk5xS5 has neither a Psk-5 nor a Psk-S phenotype, but a Psk-1 phenotype (Figure 4—source data 2).
evidence: This is based on crossing data.

claim: Multiple killing loci are involved in the Psk phenotypes.
source: This is only possible if multiple killing loci are involved, which is concordant with the observation of multiple Spok genes in these strains.
evidence: This is inferred from the phenotypic observation.

claim: The location of Spok3 and/or Spok4 of each parental strain has a corresponding introgressed SNP tract in the corresponding S5 backcross.
source: Importantly, the location of Spok3 and/or Spok4 of each parental strain has a corresponding introgressed SNP tract in the corresponding S5 backcross, while all backcrossed strains possess the Spok2 gene from strain S (Figure 4—figure supplement 3).
evidence: This is shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 3.

claim: All backcrossed strains possess the Spok2 gene from strain S.
source: Importantly, the location of Spok3 and/or Spok4 of each parental strain has a corresponding introgressed SNP tract in the corresponding S5 backcross, while all backcrossed strains possess the Spok2 gene from strain S (Figure 4—figure supplement 3).
evidence: This is shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 3.

claim: The change in the killing phenotype of Psk5xS5 can be attributed to the presence of Spok2.
source: The Psk-5 parental strain of Psk5xS5 (strain Y) does not possess Spok2, whereas Psk5xS5 does. Hence, the change in the killing phenotype of the backcrossed strain can be attributed to the presence of Spok2 (see below).
evidence: This is inferred from the comparison of Spok content.

claim: The total Spok gene content is responsible for the killer phenotype of Psk-1, Psk-2, Psk-5, and Psk-7.
source: Taken together, these data suggest that the total Spok gene content is responsible for the killer phenotype of Psk-1, Psk-2, Psk-5, and Psk-7 (Figure 4).
evidence: This is concluded from the genomic and crossing data.

claim: Psk-8 can be described by Spok gene content and position.
source: In addition, we determined (on the basis of experimental crosses) that the newly described Psk-8 type can also be described by Spok gene content and position (Figure 4—source data 2 and 3).
evidence: This is based on crossing data.

claim: Psk-8 has the same Spok block position as Psk-7, but does not possess Spok3.
source: Specifically, Psk-8 has the same Spok block position as Psk-7, but does not possess Spok3 (Figure 4).
evidence: This is shown in Figure 4.

claim: Spok3 and Spok4 are present in the Spok block.
source: When present, the Spok block was found once per genome and always contained at least one Spok gene.
evidence: This is based on genomic assembly data.

claim: The Spok block has clear boundaries.
source: Whole-genome alignments revealed that the Spok block has clear boundaries, and is localized at different chromosomal positions on chromosome 3 or on either arm of chromosome 5 in different strains of P. anserina (Table 1).
evidence: This is based on whole-genome alignment data.

claim: The Spok block is localized at different chromosomal positions on chromosome 3 or on either arm of chromosome 5 in different strains of P. anserina.
source: Whole-genome alignments revealed that the Spok block has clear boundaries, and is localized at different chromosomal positions on chromosome 3 or on either arm of chromosome 5 in different strains of P. anserina (Table 1).
evidence: This is shown in Table 1.

claim: In P. pauciseta (CBS237.71), the Spok block is found on chromosome 4.
source: In P. pauciseta (CBS237.71), the Spok block is found on chromosome 4.
evidence: This is based on genomic data.

claim: The Spok blocks of the different strains share segments and overall structure.
source: The Spok blocks of the different strains share segments and overall structure (Figure 5 and Figure 5—figure supplement 2), which suggests that they have a shared ancestry.
evidence: This is shown in Figure 5.

claim: The Spok blocks have a shared ancestry.
source: The Spok blocks of the different strains share segments and overall structure (Figure 5 and Figure 5—figure supplement 2), which suggests that they have a shared ancestry.
evidence: This is inferred from the shared structure.

claim: Within the Spok block, a given strain can harbor either or both of Spok3 and Spok4.
source: Within the Spok block, a given strain can harbor either or both of Spok3 and Spok4, and the regions containing the Spok genes appear to represent a duplication event (Figure 5).
evidence: This is shown in Figure 5.

claim: The regions containing the Spok genes appear to represent a duplication event.
source: Within the Spok block, a given strain can harbor either or both of Spok3 and Spok4, and the regions containing the Spok genes appear to represent a duplication event (Figure 5).
evidence: This is inferred from the structure shown in Figure 5.

claim: Strain TG+ shows an additional duplication that has resulted in a second copy of Spok3.
source: Strain TG+ shows an additional duplication that has resulted in a second copy of Spok3 (Figure 5—figure supplement 2).
evidence: This is shown in Figure 5—figure supplement 2.

claim: All Psk interactions can be explained by the presence, absence, or location of Spok2, Spok3, and Spok4.
source: Our classifications, based on crosses, show that the killing hierarchy observed in the Wageningen population of P. anserina is an emergent property of the presence and absence of the various Spok homologs in the different genomes.
evidence: This is concluded from crossing experiments.

claim: Other components of the Spok block do not affect spore-killing.
source: Hence, our data demonstrate that other components of the Spok block do not affect spore-killing.
evidence: This is concluded from the crossing experiments.

claim: Crosses between Psk-1 and Psk-7 strains show mutual resistance.
source: As an example, in a cross between strains of Psk-1 and of Psk-7 killer types, there is spore-killing. However the F1 progeny from this cross show no killing when crossed to either parent, nor when selfed, satisfying condition 2. Thus they are mutually resistant, which is consistent with the fact that they carry the same three Spok genes.
evidence: This is based on crossing data.

claim: Psk-7 is dominant to Psk-8.
source: An example in which the Psks show dominance is in the interaction between Psk-7 and Psk-8, which is revealed by the absence of killing when an F1 progeny from a Psk-7 x Psk-8 cross is selfed or crossed to the Psk-7 parent, and the observation of killing when crossed to the Psk-8 parent.
evidence: This is based on crossing data.

claim: Spok2 is completely associated with two-spored asci in crosses between Psk-1 and Psk-5 strains.
source: We confirmed that Spok2 is completely associated with two-spored asci in these crosses using a pooled sequencing approach (Figure 4—figure supplement 5), an observation that is in line with the backcrossing results.
evidence: This is confirmed by pooled sequencing data shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 5.

claim: Three-spored asci are probably due to incomplete penetrance of the killing factor.
source: Therefore, the three-spored asci are probably due to incomplete penetrance of the killing factor and support the conclusion that the spore killing observed in these crosses is caused by the same gene, Spok2.
evidence: This is inferred from the observation of three-spored asci and isolation of spores from them.

claim: Spok1 is dominant over Psk-S and Psk-2 strains.
source: Although TD shows low fertility with P. anserina (Boucher et al., 2017), we were successful in mating TD to a number of P. anserina strains of different Psk spore-killer types (Figure 4—source data 2 and 3). Often, only a few perithecia were produced with limited numbers of asci available to count, but despite this obstacle, the crosses clearly demonstrate that TD is dominant over Psk-S and Psk-2 strains, and is mutually resistant to a Psk-5 strain.
evidence: This is based on crossing data.

claim: Spok1 is mutually resistant to Psk-5 strains.
source: Although TD shows low fertility with P. anserina (Boucher et al., 2017), we were successful in mating TD to a number of P. anserina strains of different Psk spore-killer types (Figure 4—source data 2 and 3). Often, only a few perithecia were produced with limited numbers of asci available to count, but despite this obstacle, the crosses clearly demonstrate that TD is dominant over Psk-S and Psk-2 strains, and is mutually resistant to a Psk-5 strain.
evidence: This is based on crossing data.

claim: Spok1 provides resistance to all of the Spok homologs in P. anserina.
source: These results imply that Spok1 provides resistance to all of the Spok homologs in P. anserina and is capable of killing in the presence of Spok2 and Spok3, but not Spok4.
evidence: This is inferred from the crossing results.

claim: Spok1 is capable of killing in the presence of Spok2 and Spok3, but not Spok4.
source: These results imply that Spok1 provides resistance to all of the Spok homologs in P. anserina and is capable of killing in the presence of Spok2 and Spok3, but not Spok4.
evidence: This is inferred from the crossing results.

claim: Spok4 provides resistance against Spok1.
source: The mutual resistance with the Psk-5 strain also demonstrates that Spok4 provides resistance against Spok1.
evidence: This is inferred from the crossing results.

claim: The Spok genes are expressed during spore-killing.
source: To investigate whether the Spok genes are expressed during spore-killing, we conducted an additional nine backcrosses of the S5 strains to S, in order to generate S14 backcrossed strains (see 'Materials and methods'). We produced RNAseq data for self-killing S14 cultures and mapped the reads to the final assemblies of the dominant killer parental strains (Figure 2—figure supplement 2A). The expression of the Spok genes is evident in this data and supports the presence of an intron in the 5' UTR of the Spok homologs (Figure 2 and Figure 2—figure supplement 2B–E).
evidence: This is shown by RNAseq data in Figure 2—figure supplement 2.

claim: There is an intron in the 5' UTR of the Spok homologs.
source: The expression of the Spok genes is evident in this data and supports the presence of an intron in the 5' UTR of the Spok homologs (Figure 2 and Figure 2—figure supplement 2B–E).
evidence: This is supported by RNAseq data shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 2.

claim: The intron in the 5' UTR is not required for spore killing.
source: We conclude from this experiment that the unspliced form of Spok3 is not required for normal killing activity, and neither does the killing and resistance function rely on an alternatively spliced form of this intron.
evidence: This is concluded from experiments with intron-deleted Spok3.

claim: The SPOK3 protein is predicted to be composed of three folded domains separated by two unstructured domains.
source: The SPOK3 protein was predicted to be composed of three folded domains (located at amino-acid positions ~ 40 to 170, 210 to 400, and 490 to 700 in the protein) separated by two unstructured domains (~170 to 210 and 400 to 490) as shown in Figure 6.
evidence: This is based on domain prediction analysis shown in Figure 6.

claim: Domain 2 of SPOK3 showed homology to a class of phosphodiesterases of the PD-(D/E)XK superfamily.
source: Domain 2 showed homology to a class of phosphodiesterases of the PD-(D/E)XK superfamily (~214 to 325) with the catalytic residues forming the PD-(D/E)XK motif spanning positions 219 to 240 in the SPOK3 sequence (Steczkiewicz et al., 2012).
evidence: This is based on HHPred analysis with citation support.

claim: Domain 3 of SPOK3 was identified as a hypothetical kinase domain.
source: Domain 3 was identified as a hypothetical kinase domain (~539 to 700) as predicted previously by Grognet et al. (2014).
evidence: This is based on domain prediction with citation support.

claim: A motif with a cluster of three highly conserved cysteine residues together with histidine residues was identified upstream of the kinase motif.
source: In addition, a motif with a cluster of three highly conserved cysteine residues together with histidine residues (C-x3-C-x13-C-x5-H-x7-H) that is reminiscent of the zinc-finger motifs was identified upstream of the kinase motif (Figure 6).
evidence: This is shown in Figure 6.

claim: D667 was identified as the catalytic base residue in the catalytic loop of the kinase domain.
source: As previously reported for Spok2, D667 was identified as the catalytic base residue in the catalytic loop (subdomain VIb) of the kinase domain.
evidence: This is based on domain analysis with implicit citation to Grognet et al., 2014.

claim: The Spok-kinase domain might be more closely related to eukaryotic-like kinases (ELKs) than to eukaryotic protein kinases (ePKs).
source: Inspection of the VIb and VII functional regions, which are informative as regards to kinase substrate specificity, suggests that the Spok-kinase domain might be more closely related to eukaryotic-like kinases (ELKs) than to eukaryotic protein kinases (ePKs), raising the possibility that this kinase domain is not necessarily a protein kinase domain and could phosphorylate other substrates (Steczkiewicz et al., 2012; Kannan et al., 2007).
evidence: This is inferred from domain analysis with citation support.

claim: Domain 2 is important for killing activity.
source: We were able to determine that domain 2 is important for killing activity whereas domain 3 is important for resistance activity.
evidence: This is concluded from mutagenesis experiments.

claim: Domain 3 is important for resistance activity.
source: We were able to determine that domain 2 is important for killing activity whereas domain 3 is important for resistance activity.
evidence: This is concluded from mutagenesis experiments.

claim: The Spok3 D667A mutant allele leads to a drastic reduction in transformation efficiency.
source: This Spok3 D667A mutant allele leads to a drastic reduction in transformation efficiency (Figure 6—source data 1), whereas the Spok3 wildtypeallele only moderately affects the number of transformants.
evidence: This is experimental data from transformation assays.

claim: The D667A mutation abolishes spore killing.
source: Four-spored asci with two white and two black spores were observed, suggesting that the D667A mutation abolishes spore killing.
evidence: This is based on crossing data.

claim: Spok3 D667A is toxic in vegetative cells.
source: This result is consistent with the observation that Spok3 D667A affects transformation efficiency and is toxic.
evidence: This is inferred from the transformation efficiency data.

claim: Spok2 and Spok1 are expressed in vegetative cells of monokaryotic cultures.
source: Moreover, we detected expression of Spok2 and Spok1 in the vegetative cells of monokaryotic (self-sterile) cultures, suggesting that Spok activity is not restricted to the sexual cycle (Figure 2—figure supplement 2C and D).
evidence: This is shown by RNAseq data in Figure 2—figure supplement 2C and D.

claim: Spok activity is not restricted to the sexual cycle.
source: Moreover, we detected expression of Spok2 and Spok1 in the vegetative cells of monokaryotic (self-sterile) cultures, suggesting that Spok activity is not restricted to the sexual cycle (Figure 2—figure supplement 2C and D).
evidence: This is inferred from the expression in vegetative cells.

claim: Spok3 D667A toxicity in vegetative cells is suppressed by co-expression with wildtype Spok3.
source: Co-transformation experiments were set up with Spok3 D667A used as the transformation vector in the presence or absence of wt Spok3. As in the previous experiment, Spok3 D667A alone was found to affect transformation efficiency, but this effect was suppressed in co-transformations with Spok3 (Figure 6—source data 1).
evidence: This is experimental data from co-transformation assays.

claim: Spok3 D667A is only toxic in the absence of Spok3.
source: This experiment confirms that Spok3 D667A is only toxic in the absence of Spok3.
evidence: This is concluded from the co-transformation experiments.

claim: The Spok-related killing and resistance activities can be recapitulated in vegetative cells.
source: Therefore, the Spok-related killing and resistance activities can be recapitulated in vegetative cells.
evidence: This is concluded from the transformation experiments.

claim: The kinase domain and the cysteine-cluster region are both required for the Spok-related resistance function but not for the killing activity.
source: These results suggest that the kinase domain and the cysteine-cluster region are both required for the Spok-related resistance function but not for the killing activity.
evidence: This is inferred from the mutagenesis experiments.

claim: Domain 3 appears to be required for the resistance function but dispensable for the killing activity.
source: If, as proposed here, the toxicity and suppression activities assayed in vegetative cells are mechanistically related to spore-killing, then domain 3 appears to be required for the resistance function but dispensable for the killing activity, which can be carried out by the N-terminal region of the SPOK3 protein (domains 1 and 2).
evidence: This is inferred from the truncation experiments.

claim: The predicted nuclease domain is required for killing activity.
source: Introduction of this point mutation in the Spok3(1--490) allele abolished its killing activity in transformation assays (Figure 6—source data 1), suggesting that the predicted nuclease domain is required for killing activity.
evidence: This is concluded from mutagenesis experiments.

claim: The K240A mutation abolishes the spore-killing activity of Spok3.
source: In the cross to ΔSpok2, no killing was observed: the majority of the asci were four-spored with two white and two black spores (308/379, 81.2%), indicating that the K240A mutation abolishes the spore-killing activity of Spok3.
evidence: This is experimental data from crosses.

claim: The Spok3 K240A allele has no killing ability but has retained resistance.
source: These crosses indicate that the Spok3 K240A allele has no killing ability but has retained resistance.
evidence: This is concluded from the crossing experiments.

claim: The mutations in the Spok2 allele of strain A fall within a conserved region of the predicted nuclease domain.
source: Grognet et al. (2014) reported that strain A bears a mutant allele of Spok2 that has affected killing ability but retains resistance. The mutations in that allele fall within a conserved region of the predicted nuclease domain (Figure 6) and map on predicted structural models in close vicinity to the catalytic lysine residue (K240 in SPOK3) and the other catalytic residues (Figure 6—figure supplement 2).
evidence: This is shown in Figure 6 and Figure 6—figure supplement 2, with citation support.

claim: The properties of the Spok2 allele of strain A provide independent evidence that the nuclease domain of SPOK proteins is involved in killing activity but dispensable for resistance.
source: Hence, the properties of the Spok2 allele of strain A provide independent evidence that the nuclease domain of SPOK proteins is involved in killing activity but dispensable for resistance.
evidence: This is inferred from the comparison with the mutant allele.

claim: A BLAST search revealed an uneven distribution of Spok-related proteins among fungal taxa.
source: A BLAST search for closely related homologs of the Spok genes across fungi revealed an uneven distribution of related proteins among taxa.
evidence: This is based on BLAST search results.

claim: No additional Spok genes were found in the Sordariales beyond those newly described in Podospora.
source: Among the available genomes from the Sordariales, we did not find any protein-coding sequences in addition to our newly described Spok genes of Podospora.
evidence: This is based on BLAST search results.

claim: Protein-coding sequences with high similarity to Spok were found across other orders of the Sordariomycetes, namely the Xylariales, Glomerellales and Hypocreales, as well as in one species of the Eurotiomycetes, Polytolypa hystricis.
source: By contrast, we found protein-coding sequences with high similarity across other orders of the Sordariomycetes, namely the Xylariales, Glomerellales and Hypocreales, as well as in one species of the Eurotiomycetes, Polytolypa hystricis (Poh; Figure 7).
evidence: This is shown in Figure 7.

claim: The SPOK phylogeny shows a high degree of incongruence with the species phylogeny.
source: These phylogenies reveal two notable patterns. First, the SPOK phylogeny shows a high degree of incongruence with the species phylogeny.
evidence: This is shown by phylogenetic analysis in Figure 7.

claim: The SPOK phylogeny can be robustly divided into two clades: Clade I and II.
source: Moreover, the SPOK phylogeny can be robustly divided into two clades: Clade I and II.
evidence: This is shown in Figure 7.

claim: Clade I contains the Fs_82228 sequence from Fusarium solani.
source: Clade I contains the Fs_82228 sequence from Fusarium solani (old name Nectria haematococca).
evidence: This is shown in Figure 7.

claim: The Fs_82228 sequence was previously introduced into P. anserina, and the genetically modified strain produced empty asci when mated to a naïve strain.
source: This sequence was previously introduced into P. anserina, and the genetically modified strain produced empty asci when mated to a naïve strain, suggesting that it has a killing action (Grognet et al., 2014).
evidence: This is stated with citation support.

claim: Clade II contains the Podospora Spok homologs.
source: Clade II contains the Podospora Spok homologs.
evidence: This is shown in Figure 7.

claim: The sequences in Clade I are present in single copies in each strain, except for Fusarium oxysporum f. sp. pisi.
source: The sequences in Clade I are present in single copies in each strain, except for Fusarium oxysporum f. sp. pisi (Fop), suggesting that they are all orthologs.
evidence: This is based on the phylogenetic analysis shown in Figure 7.

claim: Many of the sequences in Clade II are present in multiple copies in each genome.
source: By contrast, many of the sequences in Clade II are present in multiple copies in each genome.
evidence: This is shown in Figure 7.

claim: Several of the duplicate Spok homologs in F. oxysporum are present on the lineage-specific chromosomes that are often associated with pathogenicity.
source: It is particularly interesting to note how many Spok homologs from Clade II are present across strains of F. oxysporum (Fo) and the number of copies that are found in each genome. Several of the duplicate Spok homologs are present on the lineage-specific chromosomes of Fusarium that are often associated with pathogenicity (Armitage et al., 2018).
evidence: This is stated with citation support.

claim: Beauveria bassiana shows a high degree of variability in homolog content among the four strains that have homologs, indicating that the homologs are polymorphic in this species.
source: Beauveria bassiana (Bb) also shows a high degree of variability in homolog content among the four strains that have homologs, indicating that the homologs are polymorphic in this species.
evidence: This is inferred from the phylogenetic data.

claim: The Clade II Spok homologs diversify within each strain or species in much the same way as the Spok genes do in Podospora.
source: The Clade II Spok homologs also appear to diversify within each strain or species in much the same way as the Spok genes do in Podospora, with variable lengths of the coil-coil repeat region and frameshift mutations near the 3′ end that relocate the stop codon.
evidence: This is based on sequence analysis.

claim: The identification of Spok3 and Spok4 has allowed explanation of the genomic basis for five of the seven Psk spore-killer types found in natural populations of P. anserina.
source: The identification of Spok3 and Spok4 has allowed us to explain the genomic basis for five of the seven Psk spore-killer types found in natural populations of P. anserina.
evidence: This is a summary of the main findings.

claim: The multiple drive elements in P. anserina involve combinations of closely related driver genes that belong to the same Spok gene family.
source: Through our integrative approach of genomics, molecular biology and phenotyping, we have been able to demonstrate that the multiple drive elements that have been genetically identified in P. anserina are not based on different underlying molecular mechanisms and/or specific gene interactions, but rather involve combinations of closely related driver genes that belong to the same Spok gene family.
evidence: This is a summary of the main findings.

claim: The Spok genes appear to be responsible for all of the identified drive elements in Podospora, with the exception of the het-s spore-killing system.
source: The Spok genes thus appear to be responsible for all of the identified drive elements in Podospora, with the exception of the het-s spore-killing system.
evidence: This is a summary conclusion.
